Here's the letter. I've kept it in your voice — warm, a bit cheeky, honest about the rough parts so the good parts land. Just swap in your name at the end (and the school name if you want it on the letterhead).

---

**Kelechi Obi**
**Croydon, London**
**10 November 2026**

Dear Kelechi,

You asked for it in writing, so here it is. In ink, on paper, posted to Croydon like a responsible adult. Put your phone down and read it on the train like you promised you would.

I'm not going to pretend this is a recruitment brochure. It isn't. It's me, writing to my friend, trying to get him to come to one meeting. There's some teasing in here (you'd be disappointed if there wasn't), and there's a section where I tell you straight what the job actually involves, because if I only sold you the good parts you'd take the whole thing to the car park and laugh at me.

But let's start with the bit that actually convinced me. Because I wasn't planning on becoming a maths teacher, and I'm not exactly a career changer, so nobody should have to take my word for it.

**Damola**

Last month I had a Year 11 boy called Damola. Simultaneous equations. The kind of thing that makes an adult maths teacher want to lie down.

Three weeks he was stuck. Three weeks of the same three questions, and I could see him starting to decide he was just bad at it, which is the most dangerous thought a fifteen-year-old boy can have. So I kept going back to it with him, one at a time, smaller and smaller pieces, until one Wednesday afternoon it turned over in his head.

He shouted — actually shouted, out loud, in front of thirty other boys — *"is that all???"*

The whole class clapped. I wish I'm making it up. I had a Year 11 boy who has spent four years being quietly sure he was stupid, and one Wednesday he found out he wasn't, and thirty children stood up and let him know.

That is the whole job. That is the entire thing I'd be asking you to walk into. Everything else is logistics.

And before you say it — yes, I know, I know. You would have shouted too. You shouted at me once over a hostel power cut, so I'm not taking any credit.

**What made me think of you**

Not the maths, actually. Or rather, not only the maths.

Last Christmas, my nephew was struggling with fractions. Nothing serious, just the usual — the boy thinks one-half of a plate of jollof rice is smaller than one-third of it, and who can blame him, the plate is enormous. And you sat down with him and did it with the actual plates. Portions of rice. Moved them around. Gave him the spoon and made him do it.

He still talks about it. Six months later, that boy brings up "the jollof rice fractions" as his favourite maths memory. Not school. Christmas. The jollof rice fractions.

Do you understand what you did there? You took a thing he was embarrassed about, and instead of explaining it to him from above, you put it in his hands and let him work it out. That's not tutoring, that's teaching. The A in Further Maths is the certificate. The jollof rice is the evidence.

**Why our school, and why now**

Because we don't have enough maths teachers and I'm sick of pretending we do. We have a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September — that's two groups of fourteen-year-olds being taught by someone who is also covering somewhere else, and who will be gone by Christmas. Our school has about eleven hundred children and I'm one of the maths teachers.

That supply post is why I'm writing to you instead of waiting. The gap is real, and it will still be real when the applications open.

**What I'd actually be asking you to do**

Come to the open evening. That's it. That is the entire ask.

**Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham.**

No application. No forms. No interviews. No commitment of any kind. It's an information evening — you go, you see who runs the training, you ask them whatever you want, you listen to what they say, and then you go home and think about it for as long as you like. I said I'd come with you and I meant it. I'll meet you outside, we'll go in together, and if it's terrible we'll leave after the biscuits and go get food, because I am not going to sit there and defend the idea to your face while you're being polite.

I'm asking you to come and look, not to sign anything. I know the difference. Nothing happens on 19 November except you find out whether the thing is real.

**If you did it: the training route**

Here's the shape of it, roughly:

- There's a salaried route. That's the one I'd point you at. You're paid while you train — you're not a student with a part-time job, you're a trainee teacher on a salary.
- One year of training.
- Starting September 2027. Applications open soon, which is why I'm writing now rather than in the spring — I want you to have seen it, had it in the back of your mind, ready to go, before the deadline sneaks up on you.

**The money, honestly**

Your pay drops in the first year. I'm not going to dress that up. A quantity surveyor on nine years is not going to be on the same money as a first-year trainee teacher, and if you have a mortgage or anything like that, that first year will be tight. I'd rather you knew that now and sat with it than found out in July.

But after that: holidays — actual school holidays, the ones that are the reason you take a job in the first place — a pension, and it goes up. Every year. You know the thing about your current job, the one you've been complaining about since 2017: nine years and you're still waiting for something to move. This one moves.

**The parts that are actually hard**

You asked me not to lie to you, so:

- **Marking is endless.** Worse than costings. At least a cost sheet tells you the answer. A pile of books does not.
- **Behaviour is wahala on some days.** Not every day. Some. There are days when a Year 9 class is a wall and you go home and think about it for hours, and you'll hear your mum's voice in your head asking why you chose this.
- **Teaching is hard.** Genuinely. It's not a performance and it's not a personality. Some days you're the best teacher in the building and some days you're the reason a kid's mum gets a phone call, and both days are the same job.
- **You start at the bottom of the pay scale** and everybody knows your name, including people who earn less than you did last week. Get that out of the way early.
- **It's a different kind of tired.** Nine years of spreadsheets tired you because the work was pointless. This tired is real, but it goes somewhere. That's a trade, not a free lunch.

**And the part I'm most likely to get roasted for**

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in the first term. Twice. Both times in the car, before I went in, because I thought I'd made a terrible mistake and I didn't know how to tell anyone.

I'm not hiding it because it's true and you should have it. It did get better. It got a lot better, and not because the job got easier — because I got better at it, and because I stopped thinking I was the only one who felt like that.

Nobody tells you that when they recruit you. They tell you about the holidays. So I'm telling you about the car park.

**On being 34**

You're not too old. A woman in my department started teaching at forty-one. She's the strongest maths teacher in the building and she is very funny about the fact that she wasted four years thinking she was too late.

You have nine years of working with adults and clients and deadlines, a maths degree with an A in Further Maths behind it, and you can hold a room of teenagers without making anybody feel stupid. You are not starting from nothing. You're starting from a lot, with a different label on it.

**The thing you said**

On your last birthday, after the food, you said: *"I just want to do something that matters before 40."*

I've been sitting on that for months, Kelechi. I didn't throw it back at you then because it was a birthday and I didn't want to be that guy.

So let me be that guy now.

Nine years of checking other people's costings. Other people's. You have spent a third of your twenties making sure that a building somebody else is paying for comes in on time — and the sum total of it is that other people's money worked out. That is not a wasted life, but I think you know it is not a *used* one. And you have six years before you turn forty, and I have watched you check spreadsheets that were never going to change anything and complain about it in the same voice you complain about everything, which is a voice that means you actually care.

A Year 9 boy in Peckham who has been written off by every adult who ever taught him — one Wednesday, he shouted *"is that all???"* and thirty children clapped, and that boy is going to sit his GCSE because of it.

That is what matters. It's not glamorous. It's not going on LinkedIn. But it's the thing.

**So**

Come on 19 November. Six o'clock, Lewisham. Come and look at the training, ask them the awkward questions, see the place.

That's it. One evening. Nothing signed, nothing promised, no career required over dinner. And if you walk out and think "no, abeg, forget it" then we'll get takeaway and I'll never mention it again — well, I will mention it, but only to annoy you.

I'm doing this because you're my friend, and because I'd rather you read this on the train and laugh at me than keep being bored in a spreadsheet for another three years. You've got the degree, you've got the patience, you've got the jollof rice fractions. The only thing you don't have is someone asking you to do it out loud.

Which, apparently, needed to be on paper.

See you on the 19th. I'll be the one outside looking slightly nervous and pretending I'm not.

Yours,

**[Your name]**

*Secondary maths teacher, Peckham, London*
*Still the one who cried in the car park*

---

**P.S.** If he comes and asks "what's the catch", the catch is: the first year is a pay cut, the marking is brutal, and a supply teacher disappears at Christmas. I've said all of it in here. Better he hears it from me on paper than from some leaflet with a stock photo of a woman pointing at a whiteboard.

**P.P.S.** Print it on decent paper. He's going to keep this, I can tell.
